title: Close enough to answer
hookLine: I am near, I answer the caller (2:186), set right inside the fasting verses
carry: near, in the middle of the fast
last: SAWM — ALLAH WANTS EASE FOR YOU.

cards: It's late afternoon in Ramadan. The fast has been long, the coffee headache came and went hours ago, and the kitchen smells of something that can't be eaten yet. Fifteen minutes to sunset.
In some homes, this is when people go quiet. Someone sits with hands open; someone else stirs the soup and whispers.
Tradition counts this hour as a time when asking is heard, partly because of a verse placed exactly here. Today: close enough to answer.

teach.b: Read the passage in order. Verse one hundred eighty-five: the month of Ramadan, ease not hardship. Verse one hundred eighty-seven: the nights of the fast, eating until the white thread of dawn shows against the black.
And between them, verse one hundred eighty-six, which isn't about fasting at all.
In Pickthall's words: “And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.”
Last year you heard how this verse skips the word say, so God answers directly. This year, look at where it was placed, and how it ends.
Read in that spot, it speaks to the hungry person: you're not only holding back; you're close.

teach.h: THE FASTING PERSON IS NOT TURNED AWAY
teach.b: A hadith in at-Tirmidhi names three people whose supplication is not turned away, and the first is the one fasting, until they break their fast.

The verse goes on: so let them respond to Me, and believe in Me, so that they may be rightly guided. The word for God answering, ujib, and the word for people responding, yastajibu, come from the same root, j-w-b.

teach.h: J-W-B: THE ANSWERING RUNS BOTH WAYS
teach.b: In the verse, the answering runs both ways: God answers the caller, and the caller is asked to answer back by trusting and acting, right among the rules for the hungry days.

how: Many Muslims spend the last minutes before breaking the fast in personal supplication, following the hadith that the fasting person's du'a is not turned away, and the placement of 2:186 among the fasting verses.

o: one who fasts through the whole month
a servant who questions a prophet
one who calls out to God in prayer, asking

games.q: near, in the fast — tap the pairs.
p: the month of Ramadan, ease not hardship

s: 2:186 is placed among the verses about fasting
a hadith in at-Tirmidhi names the fasting person among those whose du'a is not turned away

games.q: fifteen minutes before sunset in Ramadan. you're hungry and tired. what do many Muslims do with this time?
games.why: they whisper du'a: the fasting person's supplication is not turned away, and 2:186 sits right in the middle of the fasting verses.

practice: If you pray, choose one thing you need and say it quietly in your own words, perhaps beginning with praise, as the Fatiha taught; if you don't, say one hope softly, so that only you hear it.
Then sit in the quiet after it, and notice how close the quiet feels.

wordCard.voice: Suppliant. The one who calls out in prayer: the one Pickthall's verse, set among the fasting verses, says God answers. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: I answer (2:186), from the root j-w-b; the same root gives yastajibu, let them respond.

carryVoice: Your line: near, in the middle of the fast. Hunger and nearness share the same hour. That's day three hundred fifty-two.

sources.q: And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3598 (three whose supplication is not turned away: the fasting person until he breaks his fast, the just ruler, the oppressed)
